title: API Resilience Runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is an iterative SRE-runbook draft for common API failure modes we see in production: client-visible timeouts, surge 429s (rate-limits), degraded streaming (partial or stalled chunk delivery), and elevated error rates (5xx/4xx anomalies). Intention: concise actionable triage + short-term mitigations an on-call engineer can use, plus notes-to-self for follow-ups and longer-term fixes.

Scope / assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood public API (hosted inference) and Dedicated control plane endpoints.
- Assumes on-call has access to PagerDuty, Slack (#sre-incident), Grafana dashboards, Kubernetes cluster access (kubectl), and logs (Cloud Logging / Loki).
- This is not the full postmortem template; see linked_artifacts for PM process.

Quick detection signals (alerts we care about):
- api-prod-latency P95 > 800ms for 5m
- rate_limit_exhausted_count spike or 429 rate > baseline by >3x
- streaming_errors rate (stream chunk failures) > 0.5%
- api_5xx_rate > SLO threshold (e.g., >1% sustained 5m)
- consumer error-rate alert from Redwood Console (route-specific)

Contact & channels:
- PagerDuty service: SRE-API-PROD
- Slack incident channel pattern: #incident-api-<yyyyMMdd>-<short>
- Escalation: primary on-call -> SRE lead (Mateo Ruiz) after 15 minutes unresolved -> Eng manager -> Product on-call if customer-impacting SLA breach

Play structure (per-incident):
1) Detect (first 5m):
   - Read the alert summary and timestamps. Capture initial scope: which routes, which regions, any customer reports.
   - Create incident Slack channel and link PagerDuty. Add tags (timeouts/429/streaming/5xx).

2) Triage (5–20m):
   - Identify blast radius: which hosts, models, customers, regions. Query dashboards:
     * Grafana: api-prod-latency, api-errors-by-code, route-specific-latency
     * Console: per-route token/success breakdown (use route filter)
   - Quick checks (order matters):
     a) Health endpoints: curl -sv "https://api.redwood.ai/_health" -> expect 200 and subsystems OK.
     b) K8s pods: kubectl get pods -n inference -o wide --selector=app=api-gateway
        kubectl describe pod <pod> if CrashLoop or OOMKilled.
     c) Ingress/edge: check envoy/nginx errors: kubectl logs -n ingress <ingress-pod> | tail -n 200 | grep -iE "timeout|429|upstream"
     d) Rate-limiter metrics: query redis/memcached counters or built-in limiter dashboards. Look for sudden bursts or config changes.
     e) Upstream model hosts: check serving pool health (kubectl get pods -l component=runner) and GPU saturations (nvidia-smi metrics in infra dashboard).

3) Mitigate (20–60m):
   - Timeouts (client-side / gateway timeouts):
     * If gateway timeouts: check upstream backlog / queue length. Consider temporarily increasing gateway timeout to give breathing room (note: risk of tie-ups). Example: restart envoy with updated timeouts via k8s rollout or apply patch to config map.
     * If upstream model is slow: shift traffic to a faster model variant or rollback recent model rollout. Use smart-routing toggles in Console to move percentage away from new variant.
     * Short-term: enable prefix/KV cache for heavy prompt families if missing.
   - 429s (rate limiting):
     * Determine if 429s are client-side (API gateway) vs downstream (model pool).
     * If gateway limiter misconfigured or a config change rolled out, revert the limiter change (k8s configmap rollback) and scale gateway pods horizontally.
     * If genuine client surge: enable global burst quota increases for trusted partners or apply emergency throttle policies: reduce per-API-key qps in Console for noisy keys.
   - Degraded streaming:
     * Symptoms: first chunk ok but subsequent chunks stall; or client sees connection reset. Check gRPC/HTTP2 connection resets and keepalive metrics.
     * Mitigations: disable streaming on affected routes (fall back to non-streaming full-response) for a subset of traffic (canary) to reduce connection pressure.
     * Check worker thread pool exhaustion on runner side; if saturated, scale runner pool or reduce concurrency.
   - Elevated error rates (5xx):
     * If 500/502/503: check upstream service (model runners) logs for OOM/GC spikes; check resource exhaustion. Scale replicas, or if recent deploy, rollback.
     * If 429-heavy causing upstream 5xx due to overwhelmed queue, pair mitigation above with increasing burst capacity or enabling degraded fallback model.

Operational commands (cheat-sheet):
- kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=api-gateway -o wide
- kubectl logs -n inference <pod> -c gateway --since=15m | grep -iE "timeout|429|5..|error"
- kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-gateway -n inference --to-revision=<n>  (if bad deploy suspected)
- curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $PD" "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/_routes?filter=..."  (query route status)
- grafana query (example): "sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=api,code=~\"5..\"}[5m])) by (route)"

Data collection (for postmortem):
- Snapshot timeframe: T-15m to T+60m from alert onset. Collect: traces, logs, route dumps, gateway configs, limiter states, and a list of significant config changes (deployments, infra scaling, feature toggles).
- Record the following as bullet points in incident channel: "affected routes, percent traffic impacted, customer-facing features, any rollback/mitigation applied, monitoring dashboard urls".

Temporary vs lasting fixes:
- Temporary: scale up replicas, rollback culprit deploy, open short-lived throttle exceptions, switch traffic to fallback model, disable streaming for canary percentage.
- Lasting: revisit rate-limiter thresholds by route, improve backpressure handling in gateway, add graceful degradation paths for streaming, add per-route circuit-breakers with clear SLOs, and add better tracing correlating request->model-runner.

Runbook entries by failure mode (concise):
- Client-visible timeouts:
  1) Confirm if gateway timeout or runner-side slowness.
  2) If gateway: check for recent envoy config changes; increase timeout as emergency and roll out a controlled change.
  3) If runner: check GPU/CPU saturation; scale pool or revert model rollout; consider enabling a faster-quantized variant.

- Persistent 429s (rate-limiting):
  1) Check limiter config and recent pushes.
  2) Identify hot API keys: run DB query or use Console to list top offenders.
  3) For top customers, consider temporary QPS bump or reduce sampling.
  4) If caused by a bug in limiter: rollback config and open a follow-up Jira.

- Degraded streaming:
  1) Look for gRPC connection resets / HTTP2 errors in ingress logs.
  2) Canary-disable streaming for affected route.
  3) If memory pressure on runner: add pod or reduce concurrency.
  4) Capture a trace of a streaming session to find where chunking stalls.

- Elevated error rates (5xx):
  1) Correlate 5xx with deploys and infra events.
  2) If correlated with deploy: rollback.
  3) If correlated with traffic spike: scale and enable fallback model.

Customer communication template (short):
- Subject: API degradation affecting [feature] — Short update
- Body: We detected an issue impacting [X%] of requests to [route]. Engineers are actively triaging; mitigations applied (rollback/scale/traffic shift). Next update in 15–30m. Reference incident channel: <link>.

Post-incident checklist (first 48h):
- Create incident ticket and assign owner for postmortem draft.
- Timeline: compile events, alerts, deploys.
- Root cause hypothesis + evidence.
- Action items with owners and due dates (e.g., change limiter thresholds, add streaming canary).
- Communication: customer outreach if SLA breached.

Notes to self / unresolved questions (work-in-progress):
- We still lack per-route streaming SLOs — add quantifiable targets and synthetic tests.
- Consider a fail-open mode for non-sensitive routes to return cached completions when model pool is saturated.
- Should we prefer increasing gateway timeouts or shifting to fallback model? Add decision framework.
- Investigate automated rollback triggers for deploys that spike 5xx beyond threshold.

Example mini postmortem skeleton (to paste into Confluence):
- Title: short descriptive incident title
- Start/End times
- Impact summary (users/routes/features)
- Root cause
- Mitigations during incident
- Long term fixes / action items
- Owners and ETA

Appendix: useful links and dashboards (fill in live links during incident):
- Grafana: api-prod-latency
- Grafana: api-errors-by-code
- Console: per-route analytics page
- PagerDuty: SRE-API-PROD

End of draft.

---
Draft notes: keep this lightweight and iteratively expand based on blameless postmortems. Add runbook automation snippets (scripts to collect logs and create incident channel) next iteration.
